clone.name: The Clone
clone.show: Season one of Halt and Catch Fire (AMC, 2014–2017) is set in 1983 Dallas: a salesman (Joe MacMillan), an engineer (Gordon Clark) and a young coder (Cameron Howe) at the fictional Cardiff Electric reverse-engineer a PC BIOS and build a portable they call the Giant.

mutiny.name: Mutiny
mutiny.show: Season two (1985–86): Cameron Howe and Donna Clark run Mutiny, a fictional online-games company working out of a Dallas house, on dial-up lines and rented mainframe time.

valley.name: The Valley
valley.show: Season three moves Mutiny to California (1986), with an IPO, an antivirus product built by Joe MacMillan and the NSFNET on the horizon; the season ends with a jump to 1990.

web.name: The Web
web.show: Season four (1990–94): the web arrives. A hand-built directory and a crawler-based search engine compete (the show calls them Comet and Rover), until the story closes around 1994.

pages.name: The BIOS Listing · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The BIOS Listing
facts: The IBM Personal Computer (model 5150) was announced on August 12, 1981.
IBM published its Technical Reference manual for the PC with the full BIOS source listing printed in it.
Power-on self test (POST): the original PC checks memory and devices at start-up and gives one short beep when all is well.
The 5150 shipped with an Intel 8088 at 4.77 MHz.

pages.name: 55 AA · The ROM Checksum · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: 55 AA · The ROM Checksum
facts: IBM PC option ROMs start with the signature bytes 55h AAh, then a length byte counted in 512-byte blocks.
The BIOS only accepts an option ROM if all its bytes sum to 0 modulo 256, so builders patch one checksum byte to make the total come out right.
Later PC and XT BIOS revisions scan roughly C8000h–F4000h in 2 KB steps for option ROMs (the very first 1981 PC BIOS did not scan for them).
IBM PC / XT BIOS ROM scan

pages.name: The Clean Room · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Clean Room
facts: Compaq was founded in February 1982 by Rod Canion, Jim Harris and Bill Murto.
Compaq got around IBM's BIOS copyright with a clean-room workalike that did every documented BIOS function but was written from scratch.
BIOS services are reached through software interrupts: INT 10h video, INT 13h disk, INT 14h serial, INT 16h keyboard, INT 17h printer, INT 1Ah time of day.
The cost of Compaq's clean-room BIOS effort is often put at about $1 million.

pages.name: The First Clones · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The First Clones
facts: Columbia Data Products' MPC 1600, released in June 1982, is counted as the first IBM PC compatible.
Eagle Computer and Corona were threatened by IBM over BIOS copyright and settled, agreeing to re-implement their BIOS.
Phoenix Technologies began licensing a clean-room PC BIOS to other makers in 1984, which opened the clone market.
Many early clones reached only partial compatibility (often quoted as about 95%) until Phoenix and others sold reverse-engineered BIOSes.

pages.name: Luggables · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Luggables
facts: The Osborne 1 (April 1981) weighed 24.5 lb, had a 5-inch screen and cost $1,795.
The Compaq Portable was announced in November 1982 and shipped in March 1983 at $2,995.
The Compaq Portable weighed 28 lb (13 kg), had a built-in 9-inch green screen and ran on AC power only.
Compaq sold 53,000 units in its first year, for $111 million in revenue, then a US business record.

pages.name: COMDEX Floor · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: COMDEX Floor
facts: COMDEX, the computer dealers' trade show, was first held in Las Vegas in 1979.
Every November COMDEX was where new PCs and clones were shown to dealers.
In the show's first season the Giant portable is unveiled at COMDEX in Las Vegas.

pages.name: 1984 · The Mac · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: 1984 · The Mac
facts: The Apple Macintosh was introduced on January 24, 1984, at $2,495.
Its "1984" TV ad, directed by Ridley Scott, aired during Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, 1984.
The Macintosh 128K had a Motorola 68000 at about 8 MHz, 128 KB of RAM and a 9-inch 512×342 black-and-white screen.

pages.name: HCF · Halt and Catch Fire · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: HCF · Halt and Catch Fire
facts: The Motorola 6800 was introduced in 1974; its incomplete opcode decoding left undocumented opcodes 9D and DD that lock the CPU until reset.
Gerry Wheeler gave them the unofficial mnemonic HCF in "Undocumented M6800 Instructions", BYTE, December 1977: the address bus turns into a 16-bit counter.
Motorola kept the behaviour in the 6802 as a quick self-test for its 128 bytes of on-chip RAM.
HCF began as a joke mnemonic; a list of "Overextended Mnemonics" with HCF ran in Creative Computing in April 1980.

pages.name: The Mutiny House · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Mutiny House
facts: CompuServe's CB Simulator (1980) was one of the first online chat services for the public.
Online time was billed by the hour; CompuServe charged $6 an hour at 300 baud and $12 at 1200 baud for games such as Island of Kesmai.
In the show, Mutiny runs its games and chat from a house in Dallas.

pages.name: CBBS · Chicago 1978 · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: CBBS · Chicago 1978
facts: CBBS, the first dial-up bulletin board system, went online in Chicago on February 16, 1978, built by Ward Christensen and Randy Suess.
Early boards took one caller at a time on one phone line.
Ward Christensen also wrote the XMODEM file-transfer protocol (1977).

pages.name: The Handshake · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Handshake
facts: The Hayes Smartmodem (1981) ran at 300 bit/s and introduced the AT command set (ATDT to dial with tones).
Bell 103 modems use frequency-shift keying: the originating side sends 1070/1270 Hz (space/mark) and the answering side 2025/2225 Hz.
Touch-tone (DTMF) digits are two tones together, one from 697/770/852/941 Hz and one from 1209/1336/1477 Hz.
By 1994 V.34 modems ran at 28.8 kbit/s.

pages.name: Fidonet · Store and Forward · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Fidonet · Store and Forward
facts: Fidonet was started in 1984 by Tom Jennings in San Francisco to pass messages between bulletin boards.
Fidonet addresses take the form zone:net/node, for example 1:102/851 (zones were added later in the 1980s).
Mail moved store-and-forward during a nightly "national mail hour", when long-distance rates were lower.

pages.name: ANSI Art · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: ANSI Art
facts: MS-DOS 2.0 (1983) added the ANSI.SYS driver, which turns ESC[ escape codes into colour and cursor moves.
ACiD Productions, one of the best-known ANSI art groups, was founded in 1990.
The 16 text colours come from the IBM PC's CGA palette.

pages.name: MUDs and Kesmai · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: MUDs and Kesmai
facts: MUD1 was written at the University of Essex in 1978 by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle.
Island of Kesmai launched on CompuServe in 1985 (Kelton Flinn recalls December 15) as a multiplayer game with roguelike graphics.
Kesmai processed one command every 10 seconds; at $6 an hour that is 1⅔ cents per command.

pages.name: Q-Link Tanks · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Q-Link Tanks
facts: Quantum Link (Q-Link), an online service for the Commodore 64 and 128, began on November 5, 1985.
Q-Link was renamed America Online in October 1989.
Lucasfilm's Habitat ran on Q-Link as a test from 1986–87, with avatars in a shared graphical world, and was relaunched as Club Caribe in 1988.

pages.name: Packet-Switched Nights · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Packet-Switched Nights
facts: Telenet (1975) and Tymnet (1971) carried dial-up users to online services over packet-switched networks.
The Erlang B formula (A. K. Erlang, 1917) gives the chance a caller hears busy, given the number of lines and the traffic.
In the show, Mutiny struggles with line capacity and rented computer time.

pages.name: Westbound · NSFNET · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Westbound · NSFNET
facts: The NSFNET backbone went live in 1986 at 56 kbit/s.
It was upgraded to T1 (1.544 Mbit/s) in 1988.
It was upgraded to T3 (45 Mbit/s) in 1991.
In the show, Mutiny moves to California in season three.

pages.name: Brain · The Boot Sector · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Brain · The Boot Sector
facts: Brain (January 1986), written by the brothers Basit and Amjad Farooq Alvi in Lahore, Pakistan, is counted as the first IBM PC virus.
Brain infects the boot sector of 360 KB floppy disks and spreads when an infected disk boots a machine.
Early antivirus products followed in 1987, including McAfee VirusScan.

pages.name: The Morris Worm · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Morris Worm
facts: The Morris worm was released on November 2, 1988, by Robert Tappan Morris.
Even when a host said it was already infected, the worm reinfected it 1 time in 7, which is why it overloaded machines.
About 6,000 of the roughly 60,000 hosts then on the internet are often said to have been hit (an estimate).
Morris was the first person convicted under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (1990).

pages.name: Black Monday · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Black Monday
facts: On Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, from 2,246.74 to 1,738.74.
That is a 22.6% drop, the largest one-day percentage fall in its history.
Tech IPOs and money worries run through the show's third season.

pages.name: The IPO Bell · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The IPO Bell
facts: Apple went public on December 12, 1980, at $22 a share.
Microsoft went public on March 13, 1986, at $21 a share.
Microsoft closed its first day at about $27.75.
In the show, Mutiny's money and its IPO become the story in season three.

pages.name: HyperCard Stacks · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: HyperCard Stacks
facts: HyperCard, created by Bill Atkinson, was released by Apple in August 1987.
It came bundled free with new Macintosh computers.
Stacks of cards with buttons that link to other cards are an early, popular form of hypertext.

pages.name: The Swap Meet · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Swap Meet
facts: eBay began as AuctionWeb, launched by Pierre Omidyar on September 3, 1995.
In a second-price (Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid, so bidding your true value is the best plan (William Vickrey, 1961).
In the show, an online swap meet is one of Mutiny's big ideas, years before real online auction sites.

pages.name: Information Management: A Proposal · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Information Management: A Proposal
facts: Tim Berners-Lee wrote "Information Management: A Proposal" at CERN in March 1989.
The first web server and browser ran on a NeXT computer at CERN by the end of 1990.
The World Wide Web project was announced publicly on August 6, 1991.
CERN put the web software into the public domain on April 30, 1993.

pages.name: Gopher Holes · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Gopher Holes
facts: Gopher was released at the University of Minnesota in 1991.
RFC 1436 (1993) describes the protocol: each menu line is a type character, a display string, a selector, a host and a port, separated by tabs.

pages.name: Archie · Search Before the Web · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Archie · Search Before the Web
facts: Archie, made in 1990 at McGill University by Alan Emtage with Bill Heelan and Peter Deutsch, indexed the file lists of public FTP sites.
Archie searched file names, not the contents of files.

pages.name: Mosaic · Pictures in the Page · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Mosaic · Pictures in the Page
facts: NCSA Mosaic's first public release (0.5) was announced by Marc Andreessen on January 23, 1993; version 1.0 followed on April 21, 1993.
Mosaic 0.10 (March 1993) added the tag for inline images.
Andreessen and Eric Bina built it at NCSA, University of Illinois; ports to Windows and the Mac came in September 1993.

pages.name: Navigator · 28.8 · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Navigator · 28.8
facts: Mosaic Communications Corporation was founded on April 4, 1994, by Jim Clark and Marc Andreessen, and renamed Netscape later that year.
Netscape Navigator's first beta came out on October 13, 1994, and version 1.0 on December 15, 1994.
Over a serial link each byte costs 10 bits (8 data bits plus start and stop bits), so a 28.8 kbit/s modem moves about 2.9 KB a second.

pages.name: Directory vs Crawler · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Directory vs Crawler
facts: Jerry Yang and David Filo started "Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web" at Stanford in January 1994; it was renamed Yahoo! a few months later.
WebCrawler, by Brian Pinkerton at the University of Washington, launched in April 1994 as the first engine to search the full text of pages.
Lycos went online at Carnegie Mellon in July 1994.
In the show's last season, a directory (Comet) and a search engine (Rover) compete.

pages.name: Eternal September · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: Eternal September
facts: Usenet started in 1979 (Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis, Duke University).
"Eternal September" names the time from September 1993, when AOL opened Usenet to its members and the new arrivals kept coming.

pages.name: NSFNET Sunset · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: NSFNET Sunset
facts: The NSFNET backbone was decommissioned on April 30, 1995, after traffic moved to commercial networks.
The commercial-traffic limits on the internet were relaxed in the early 1990s, and dial-up ISPs grew around them.
The Erlang B formula gives the busy-signal rate for a modem pool.

pages.name: The Next Thing · Halt and Catch Fire in pixels
pages.title: The Next Thing
facts: Linus Torvalds announced Linux on August 25, 1991.
Halt and Catch Fire ends its story around 1994 (series finale aired October 2017).
